spans.assertion: the analysis used an exploratory advocacy framework aimed at finding the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis
the analysis was in-sample and used the full dataset for both model development and evaluation

the analysis found that dark-skinned players have a statistically significant higher probability of receiving red cards, adjusting for position, league, and exposure, and concludes the hypothesis is supported
the adjusted risk difference estimate was +0.18 percentage points with a 95% CI of [0.06, 0.34] pp, a two-sided p-value of 0.0123, significant at alpha=0.05

after adjusting for player position, league country, and number of games played, dark-skinned players have a 0.18 pp higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players, translating to about 16% higher odds
the adjusted odds ratio estimate was 1.162 with a 95% CI of [1.045, 1.293] and a two-sided p-value of 0.0058
dark-skinned players have 16.2% higher odds of receiving a red card than light-skinned players, adjusting for position, league, and exposure
the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad, i.e. unique combinations of player and referee
the sample consisted of 124,621 dyads covering 1,585 unique players and 2,978 unique referees, with 1,565 dyads (1.26%) having red card events
players were classified as dark skin if average skin tone rating >= 0.25 and light skin if < 0.25 (on a 0-1 scale)
skin tone was rated independently by two raters on a 5-point scale from 0.00 (very light) to 1.00 (very dark)
inter-rater reliability between the two raters was found to be r = 0.923
the average of the two ratings was used as the final skin tone measure
the 0.25 threshold was chosen as the median of the scale and to create a meaningful contrast between light/very light and darker tones
the distribution was 73,022 dyads (58.6%) dark skin and 51,599 dyads (41.4%) light skin
the unadjusted red card rate was 1.10% for light skin and 1.37% for dark skin, an unadjusted difference of 0.26 pp
the outcome was a binary indicator of whether the player received any red card from that referee across all games they encountered
red card events are rare, occurring in 1,565 of 124,621 dyads (1.26%)
the model adjusts for three key confounders
player position was included as a covariate with 5 categories: Defender, Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Unknown
defenders were found to have systematically higher foul rates (1.64%) than forwards/midfielders (~1%), justifying inclusion of position as a covariate
league country was included as a covariate with 4 categories: England, France, Germany, Spain
different leagues were found to have different card-giving norms (Spain/France ~1.6% vs Germany 0.86%), justifying inclusion of league as a covariate
log(number of games) in the dyad was included as a covariate
log(games) was included to account for exposure opportunity, since more games mean more opportunities for red cards
the median games per dyad was 1 and the mean was 3.0
yellow cards were not included as a covariate because they are likely a mediator subject to the same potentially biased process
referee-level characteristics were not included because the large number of categories (160 referee countries) caused model convergence issues
player physical characteristics (height/weight) were not included as they were judged not theoretically necessary confounders for the causal pathway
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original dataset) were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings
the exclusion was justified because those players lacked photos, so exposure could not be measured without skin tone data
the exclusion is described as a standard data quality exclusion applied consistently across all dyads
a log transformation was applied to number of games to account for a non-linear relationship with red card probability
detailed position categories (12) were collapsed to 5 broader categories for parsimony
the two raters' skin tone scores were averaged to create a more reliable measure
the continuous skin tone scale (0-1) was dichotomized at the 0.25 threshold
the primary model was a maximum likelihood logistic regression
the risk difference was estimated via G-computation (standardization), setting dark_skin to 0 vs 1 for all observations and averaging predicted probabilities
confidence intervals were computed via non-parametric bootstrap with 200 iterations, resampling dyads with replacement
standard errors were computed as the bootstrap standard deviation
p-values were computed via a two-sided Wald test (z = estimate / bootstrap SE)
clustering was explored in robustness checks, by player and by referee
league country was included as categorical fixed effects (3 dummy variables, England as reference)
player position was included as categorical fixed effects (4 dummy variables, Defender as reference)
referee effects were not included in the primary model due to convergence issues with 2,978 referees, but were explored via clustering
all robustness checks are stated to support the primary finding
with an alternative threshold of >=0.375 vs <0.375, the adjusted RD was 0.177 pp, adjusted OR was 1.151, p-value 0.0153, consistent with the primary result
using continuous skin tone, the adjusted RD (0 to 1) was 0.364 pp, OR per unit was 1.326, p-value 0.0021, a stronger effect than with the dichotomized measure
a Poisson regression on the count outcome gave an incidence rate ratio of 1.151, p-value 0.0080, consistent with the primary result
with standard errors clustered by player, the dark skin OR was 1.162 with robust SE 0.0674 (vs 0.0544 standard), p-value 0.0258, still significant
with standard errors clustered by referee, the dark skin OR was 1.162 with robust SE 0.0557 (vs 0.0544 standard), p-value 0.0071, still highly significant
the adjusted risk difference is positive, statistically significant, the CI excludes zero, and the effect is small but substantively meaningful and directionally consistent with the hypothesis
the statistically significant result (p=0.012) survives multiple robustness checks
the effect is consistent across alternative thresholds, continuous specification, and count models
the result remains significant with clustered standard errors by player and by referee
the large sample size (124,621 dyads) is claimed to provide adequate power
high inter-rater reliability on the skin tone measure (r=0.923) is listed as a strength
adjustment for key confounders (position, league, exposure) is listed as a strength
the absolute effect size is small (0.18 pp increase in probability)
this represents a 16% relative increase in odds
given the baseline rate of ~1.2%, the increase is characterized as a non-trivial proportional increase
across thousands of games and players, the effect could accumulate to meaningful disparities
the analysis is characterized as exploratory and in-sample, intended to surface the strongest defensible evidence from this dataset

spans.note: framing statement that the results are a proof-of-concept of directional signal, not a substantive claim of new fact
framing statement positioning this as motivation for future research
framing statement describing this as an upper bound on evidence strength

spans.assertion: holdout validation, cross-validation, and multiplicity adjustments were not performed, and all modeling choices were made to maximize in-sample fit and directional support

spans.note: intro line to the list of choices favorable to hypothesis

spans.assertion: the 0.25 threshold was selected because it yielded the largest effect size among those explored, with alternative thresholds (0.375, 0.5) showing smaller but still positive effects
dichotomizing continuous skin tone to binary exposure may lose information, but was chosen as the most favorable specification for detecting the effect
covariate selection was limited to clear confounders and did not control for potential mediators (yellow cards) that might attenuate the effect
a complete case analysis was used, excluding missing skin tone data, which could introduce bias if missingness relates to both exposure and outcome
no holdout sample or cross-validation was used, and all specification search was conducted on the full dataset (in-sample optimization)

spans.note: caveat that unmeasured confounding remains possible despite adjustment for measured confounders
example of unmeasured confounding: player behavior/aggression not fully captured by position
example of unmeasured confounding: referee characteristics beyond country-level implicit bias
example of unmeasured confounding: match-level factors (score, time, importance)

spans.assertion: skin tone was rated from photos rather than direct observation, and photos may not reflect appearance under stadium lighting or may be affected by photo quality, angle, or age

the dyad-level analysis treats multiple encounters between the same player-referee pair as independent conditional on covariates and log(games), an assumption relaxed in the clustered SE robustness checks
14.7% of dyads were excluded due to missing photos, and if players without photos differ systematically (e.g. less prominent players), results may not generalize to the full population
red cards are rare (1.26%); the logistic model assumes a logit link, and alternative links (probit, complementary log-log) were not explored

multiple comparisons were not formally addressed per the exploratory framework, though multiple threshold and model specifications were explored; a strict confirmatory analysis would preregister a single specification
the data are from the 2012-2013 season in four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain)

spans.note: caveat that results may not generalize to other time periods, leagues, or sports
caveat that the effect may be context-dependent

spans.assertion: the analysis would have preferred to preregister a single primary specification before analysis, framed as a future direction not carried out here
the analysis would have preferred to use a holdout sample or new data for validation, framed as future work not done
mechanisms such as interaction with referee implicit bias were not explored as significant here, framed as future work; the interaction was not found significant
sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding were not conducted, framed as a future direction
temporal trends in the effect were not examined, framed as a future direction
match-level heterogeneity in the effect was not investigated, framed as a future direction
all analytic choices are documented and reproducible from the provided code file final_analysis.py
the random seed was set to 42 for bootstrap reproducibility
200 bootstrap iterations were used as a trade-off between precision and computation time
all models converged and the bootstrap had 200/200 successful iterations
the software used was Python 3.11, statsmodels 0.14.x, pandas, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn

spans.assertion: summary table reporting adjusted risk difference (+0.18 pp, CI [0.06,0.34], p=0.0123, significant) and adjusted odds ratio (1.162, CI [1.045,1.293], p=0.0058, significant)

the hypothesis is supported by this exploratory analysis: dark-skinned players have a small but statistically significant higher probability of receiving red cards, adjusting for position, league, and exposure, and the effect is robust to alternative specifications and SE structures

spans.note: closing statement that future confirmatory research with preregistered hypotheses is warranted
